text: We've covered how each platform structures its procedural blocks and declares its variables. Now let's branch and loop. If, case, and loops all exist on every platform here, but the keywords and the closing syntax are different enough to trip up anyone moving between them — and there's one real surprise waiting in this lesson about loops specifically.

T-SQL's if-else is the odd one out structurally. If at price greater than five hundred, begin, print premium, end, else, begin, print standard, end. Notice there's no end-if anywhere — T-SQL has no way to close a whole if-else statement as one unit. Every branch that has more than one statement needs its own begin-end wrapper around it.

PL/SQL and Postgres's PL slash pgsql both do this the same way, and it's cleaner. If price greater than five hundred then dbms output put line premium, elsif price greater than one hundred then mid-range, else standard, end if. One word, e-l-s-i-f, and the whole thing closes with end if. MySQL does the same idea but spells it e-l-s-e-i-f, one word, no space — a small but very real difference that catches people.

Here's the surprise. T-SQL has no native for loop. None. If you want to repeat something ten times with a counter, your only option is while plus a variable you declare and increment yourself: declare at i int equals one, while at i less than or equal ten, begin, print at i, set at i equals at i plus one, end. Compare that to PL/SQL's for i in one dot dot ten loop — no counter variable, no manual increment, the loop just handles it. Postgres's PL slash pgsql has the exact same real for loop. T-SQL developers coming from almost any other language find this genuinely surprising.

MySQL doesn't have a real for loop either, but it does have something the other three don't: repeat until. Set i equals one, repeat, select i, set i equals i plus one, until i greater than ten, end repeat. The key difference from while is that repeat checks its condition after the body runs, so the body always executes at least once, even if the condition is already false going in.

So remember this one clearly: PL/SQL and PL slash pgsql both have a genuine counting for loop; T-SQL and MySQL do not. T-SQL falls back to while plus a counter, and MySQL adds repeat-until as its own post-condition option. Next lesson, we put a lot of this together and write one real stored procedure two different ways — T-SQL and PL/SQL, side by side, parameter for parameter. See you there.
